title: Recovery Logs, Backups and Restore Drills
description: Understand redo, undo, checkpoints and binary-log point-in-time recovery, then solve restore-boundary and missing-log drills with measurable RPO and RTO.

questions.question_text: Which event is ordinarily addressed by engine crash recovery?
options: A server crash with interrupted transactional work
Every valid committed operator mistake automatically
A missing external invoice without evidence
Loss of every independent backup copy
questions.explanation: Crash recovery resolves engine state under its persistence contract.

questions.question_text: What does the write-ahead principle order?
options: A full backup before every SELECT
Required log persistence before dependent data-page persistence
Every replica before every local read
questions.explanation: The durable log must support recovery of a page that can reach storage.

questions.question_text: What is a principal use of redo?
options: Reconstruct recorded engine changes during recovery
questions.explanation: Redo records support engine recovery rather than every operational recovery goal.

questions.question_text: What can undo support?
options: Guaranteed restoration after losing all copies
Rollback and reconstruction of older row versions
questions.explanation: Undo participates in transaction rollback and consistent version reads.

questions.question_text: What does an ordinary rollback demonstration establish?
options: The demonstrated transaction reverses its supported pending changes
questions.explanation: A normal session rollback is narrower evidence than crashing and restarting a documented server.

questions.question_text: Is a checkpoint a separately protected full backup?
options: Only when a table has a primary key
Only when the client is disconnected
questions.explanation: Checkpoint progress and an independent backup have different purposes.

questions.question_text: Which sources commonly support point-in-time recovery?
options: A suitable base backup and a contiguous binary-log history
questions.explanation: The backup supplies the initial state and logs supply subsequent history.

questions.question_text: What does RPO describe?
options: The number of columns in redo
The name of a restore utility
The targeted tolerance for recent data loss
questions.explanation: Recovery point objective states a target rather than proof that it has been met.

questions.question_text: What does RTO describe?
options: The targeted time to restore the required service
The duration of every SQL statement
The size of a primary key
The maximum width of a row
questions.explanation: Recovery time objective concerns service restoration within a defined boundary.

questions.question_text: What is a suitable place to validate a restoration first?
options: A live table chosen at random
questions.explanation: Isolation permits validation without overwriting the operating service.

questions.question_text: A valid T1 precedes mistaken T2 and valid T3. Stopping before T2 also excludes what?
questions.explanation: A timeline boundary omits later events unless they are separately reconciled.

questions.question_text: The first required binary log is missing. What can be claimed?
options: Newer logs always reconstruct the missing one
The same contiguous replay point is not established
All recent transactions are definitely restored
questions.explanation: A missing dependency breaks the evidence for the planned replay chain.

questions.question_text: Does a backup job reporting success prove restoration works?
options: Only if its filename is short
Only if it ran at midnight
No, an actual restore drill is needed
questions.explanation: Creation and successful recovery are separate observations.

questions.question_text: A client reads five before rollback from a starting seven. What should it see afterward?
questions.explanation: The supported decrement was pending and is reversed by rollback.

questions.question_text: Why protect binary logs and backup copies?
questions.explanation: Secondary recovery artifacts can expose the same sensitive contents as the primary database.

questions.question_text: What should a replay boundary respect?
options: Only a convenient approximate clock time
Reviewed complete-transaction boundaries and backup coordinates
questions.explanation: Partial or misaligned replay can break the intended recovered state.

questions.question_text: What does relaxed persistence change?
options: The definition of a primary key
The failure guarantees that must be evaluated
questions.explanation: Actual durability depends on documented settings and storage behavior.

questions.question_text: A server accepts a connection after restart. Has business recovery necessarily finished?
options: No, workflow and integrity checks can remain
Only if the table count is even
questions.explanation: Database readiness and usable business service are different milestones.

questions.question_text: What should a failed recovery drill report?
options: Measured reachable point, elapsed time and unmet objectives
Only the size of the log directory
questions.explanation: Honest failure evidence supports correction without overstating recovery capability.

questions.question_text: Does redo on the same lost disk replace an independent backup?
options: Only after changing a query alias
questions.explanation: Losing the only data and recovery history together defeats that local source.

coding_not_applicable: Recovery requires a controlled server lifecycle, a backup/log chain and an isolated restoration target. The notes provide worked rollback and recovery-planning exercises; a single-query judge cannot verify crash or restore behavior.

notes:
## Separate restarting a server from recovering a business service

Database recovery brings a system to a usable state after a failure while preserving its specified guarantees. Restarting an InnoDB server after a process crash is one problem. Reconstructing yesterday's database after losing the machine is another. Recovering to the moment before an accidental committed update is different again. A plan that succeeds for the first problem may have no answer to either of the others.

Imagine an equipment desk recording checkouts. A power failure interrupts an update while a later incident deletes a set of committed checkout rows. Crash recovery should handle the interrupted transactional state under the engine's persistence contract. It will not ordinarily interpret a valid committed deletion as an operator mistake and undo it automatically. That second incident requires a separately planned restoration and replay decision, using evidence of the desired recovery boundary.

## Use write-ahead reasoning to understand redo

InnoDB modifies pages in memory and eventually writes dirty pages to data files. Redo records describe changes needed for recovery. The write-ahead principle requires the relevant log information to reach the required durable state before modified data pages are allowed to make that information necessary for recovery. This ordering lets recovery reason about pages that were not all flushed together at the instant of a crash.

Durability depends on actual persistence settings and storage guarantees. A returned COMMIT under one configuration need not have the same power-loss behavior as a returned COMMIT under a relaxed configuration. Hardware caches, filesystem behavior and binary-log synchronization also matter. Do not teach a successful client response as proof that every failure scope, including total storage loss, has been covered by one local log.

Redo is not a substitute for a backup. Losing the data directory and the only local redo files together can leave no independent source from which to restore the service. Likewise, possession of a backup file does not prove that its dependencies, encryption access and recovery instructions still work. Evidence comes from an authorized restore drill on an isolated target, not merely from a scheduled job reporting that a file was written.

## Distinguish undo and version visibility

Undo information supports reversing uncommitted transactional changes and supports consistent-read reconstruction of earlier row versions. It therefore participates in both recovery and normal concurrent reading. Redo and undo are complementary concepts rather than two names for the same history file. The engine may need to reconstruct recorded changes and then resolve work belonging to transactions that did not commit.

A simple transaction illustrates the difference between pending and committed effects. In a disposable lab, begin with seven available devices, subtract two and deliberately roll back. The final committed quantity should remain seven. Repeating the same decrement and committing establishes five as the intended new quantity. Merely reading five inside the first transaction did not establish a durable committed outcome.

```sql
START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE recovery_lab SET available=available-2 WHERE asset_id=1;
SELECT available FROM recovery_lab WHERE asset_id=1;
ROLLBACK;
SELECT available FROM recovery_lab WHERE asset_id=1;
```

The fragment assumes a transactional fixture containing asset one with quantity seven. It predicts five before rollback and seven afterward. A later crash experiment requires an actual controlled server lifecycle, documented persistence settings and independent inspection after restart. Do not claim that a normal rollback demonstration has tested crash recovery or that killing an unrelated production process is a reasonable teaching shortcut.

## Explain checkpoints without imagining a full backup

A checkpoint records progress that helps bound how much log work recovery must consider. Dirty-page flushing and log reuse are coordinated with this progress. A checkpoint is not a user-visible snapshot of every table and does not generally mean all transactions have stopped and all data has been copied to a separate safe location. Confusing these ideas leads to unreliable recovery expectations.

Recovery time also depends on workload, outstanding dirty pages, hardware and the engine's recovery work. A smaller redo interval can reduce one component without guaranteeing a specific recovery duration. Measure the entire service restoration path: database restart, integrity checks, application readiness and business reconciliation. A server accepting a TCP connection does not establish that the equipment desk can safely resume processing checkouts.

## Combine a suitable backup with binary-log replay

Point-in-time recovery commonly restores a suitable full backup, then replays the retained binary-log history from the backup's recorded coordinate to a chosen boundary. The backup and logs must form a consistent chain. Missing an earlier required log cannot normally be repaired by possessing several newer logs. Retention must cover the interval in which recovery might be requested, including time spent discovering the incident.

Binary logs serve a different role from InnoDB redo. They record a server-level change history used for replication and point-in-time recovery; redo supports engine crash recovery. The exact logging format, transaction boundaries and coordinates influence replay. Restore tooling must understand how the backup was taken and where replay begins. Never invent a log position from a wall-clock estimate or replay an arbitrary partial transaction simply because its timestamp looks convenient.

| Recovery source | Primary purpose in this explanation | Important limitation |
|---|---|---|
| Redo | Recover recorded engine changes after a crash | Does not replace an independent backup |
| Undo | Resolve uncommitted changes and older versions | Does not reverse every committed mistake on request |
| Full backup | Restore an earlier database state | Needs compatible preparation and validation |
| Binary logs | Replay subsequent history to a reviewed boundary | Requires an unbroken suitable log chain |

## Choose the incident boundary deliberately

Suppose a backup represents a known state before transactions T1, T2 and T3. T1 is a valid checkout, T2 is the accidental deletion and T3 is another valid action. Replaying through T1 and stopping before T2 excludes the deletion but also excludes T3 from that restored timeline. Recovering T3's business effect can require separate reconciliation. Skipping selected events casually can violate dependencies that later actions assumed.

Perform recovery on an isolated target first. Inspect event boundaries, validate the chosen stop point and compare the restored rows with independent business evidence. Protect backups and logs because they can contain sensitive information even if the public application never exposes that information. Recovery access, temporary copies and eventual cleanup deserve the same deliberate controls as the primary database.

## Define RPO and RTO with measurable boundaries

Recovery point objective describes the tolerated loss of recent data, often expressed as time. Recovery time objective describes the targeted time to restore the required service. They are objectives, not observations automatically satisfied by enabling a setting. A fifteen-minute backup interval alone does not prove a fifteen-minute recovery point when backups fail silently or required logs expire before an incident is detected.

A useful drill records the incident time, selected recovery point, start of restoration, completion of database checks and time the intended workflow becomes usable. Include delays for obtaining authorized access and loading necessary keys through approved processes without copying secret values into the drill report. Report actual measured loss and elapsed time separately from the objectives so an unsuccessful drill still produces useful engineering evidence.

## Include integrity and dependency checks

After restoration, verify more than a row count. Compare important totals, required relationships and the status of in-flight business requests. A matching total can hide different missing and duplicated rows. Confirm that scheduled jobs and message delivery remain paused until the recovered database has a reviewed role in the service, so validation does not accidentally send duplicate notifications.

## Solve two recovery planning exercises

First exercise: a base backup ends at coordinate B, retained logs cover B through E, and the erroneous transaction begins at reviewed boundary D. Describe a safe recovery plan. The solution restores the backup to an isolated target and replays the contiguous history from B up to the chosen complete-transaction boundary before D, then validates rows and constraints before any cutover decision. It does not replay the mistaken transaction merely to reach the newest timestamp.

Second exercise: the team has a backup but the first required log is missing. Can it promise the same recovery point? The solution is no: the gap prevents a justified contiguous replay claim. Investigate another valid backup or log copy, state the reachable point honestly and reconcile missing business work. Link these decisions to [durability](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/durability), [rollback](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/rollback) and [transaction states](/learning/dbms-sql-tutorial/transaction-states). A recovery plan is complete only for the failure scopes and drills it has actually demonstrated.
